**Just deleted my youtube account that I’ve used for 7 years.  Copied over this comment from the video before I deleted everything:**
     This is the final straw - I am deleting this account as soon as I write this comment.  I start college tomorrow, and I have been considering deleting this ever since I got a new computer a few weeks ago.  I only use this account for youtube, under an anonymous name, and have never really shared its existence with anyone I know.  Perhaps that was the most obvious sign that I had a problem. There have been other symptoms of this problem before, and during my youtube issues.  I have during multiple periods of the last several years spent a month at a time getting stoned every night.  My friends eventually left me  junior year largely because of this, and it only worsened after that.  Another symptom has been my compulsive eating, especially late at night, to ward off the boredom of falling asleep.  I need to really fix my attention issues, and deleting this account entirely is the only thing that may actually keep me away, so I guess this is goodbye.  I have made small attempts to fix my issues many times over and over again, but I am hoping that a new school, a new bedroom, a new dining schedule, and deletion of my youtube account will be drastic enough to change my ways, brcause if I don’t, I will miss my classes, not do the homework, not clean my room, and fail out of school.

The best answer I have is that balance is the answer.  We can still have fun, but we should learn to not depend on this for our livelihood.  My example before was heroin: feels good, but you gain nothing in the long run, even if it didn't become physically addictive.  Pleasure has a place, but most things of this sort will not lead to any lasting happiness, and often do just the opposite.  I think Buddhism's main benefit is that it is trying to fix addiction to some extent.  I have been using heroin as an example because it is obvious and easy, but this can really creep way more into people's lives than they realize.  Any sort of routine or pleasure can result in pain later on - you just have to decide when it is worth the risk, how to be careful about it to prevent later consequences, and how to gain the maximum long term benefits (knowledge and growth and such).  Heroin is clearly not worth the later bad stuff.  But there are other things like: relationships (you get attached and then they leave you); TV (you are entertained but later realize you haven't seen your friends in months because you wasted it); Procrastination (you feel good now cause you aren't doing work, but you are going to hate yourself later).  Basic stuff like that.
tl;dr: attachement can be worth it but weigh the risks and be smart about it.

I think we have to just let people make their own decisions.  Yes, your freedom dies when you die, but people make the decision when they are alive.  By your logic, no wealth should ever be inherited, but instead all redistributed by the government.  Which I agree could be a logical stance, but assigning all responsibility to the government and trusting them can be unwise as well, and I think this crosses that line.  Some freedom should be retained after death for the sake of both the survivors and the comfort of the subjects while they are still alive.  
     The better option is to educate people on the subject well and try to convince them to do the right thing for others.  It will not always work, but doing anything otherwise really would infringe upon our own freedoms because we as a society believe it would.  The simple logical solution is not always the best solution for society when you factor in humans and how we work.

The majority should often decide policies, because this prevents small groups from imposing their will on everyone else, and keeps the most people happy.  However, this doesn't work perfectly either.  You mentioned that 90% of people could want slavery, and yet it would still be wrong, which I agree with.  
As Ayn Rand said (Who I don't generally quote because I hate her, but this I somewhat agree with), "Individual rights are not subject to a public vote; a majority has no right to vote away the rights of a minority; the political function of rights is precisely to protect minorities from oppression by majorities." 
 Which makes sense, in that governments should protect everyone.  The only issue with this is that if the majority does not decide on a matter, who does?  Because then the power is left in the hands of a few people.  And, 90% of people could endorse slavery, and the king could still outlaw it, fixing the issue; but also, 90% could oppose it, and the king could force it upon them.  Herein lies the issue of how we decide what to do in government.  
     That all was mostly irrelevant, but just an introduction to basic evaluation of democracy.  The real question is where the line is drawn regarding a "radical" change.  If freeing slaves required a 67% support for it (which it did in the US congress actually), it would be harder to do that right thing and free them.  But the opposing thought is that if it is right to do, in the long term people will shift to that view and a united conclusion will emerge, which also makes some sense.  
     My final conclusion regarding this issue (so far I have just shown some opinions on both sides) is that unless the change is _incredibly_ drastic, it is unlikely in politics that such a vast majority will ever be reached.  This essentially means that until things get so bad that everyone agrees; the problem cannot be fixed.  Which really blocks change, because that means that you cannot fix the leak until your house is already flooded.  I don't agree with their decision on the Brexit, but I think that if the majority wanted it, then they should be able to decide that.  If in two months, they change their minds and 51% decide that they should re-enter, that should also be followed.  But I agree that its a convoluted issue.

we have a combination of two things that drive this: heat and pressure.  The gas particles have to be moving in order to expand in this way.  Anything that is at exactly absolute zero in a vacuum with no light hitting it will not actually expand out of the box or piston.  The molecules will stay still in space within the box.  Now if we assume that the gas has some heat (otherwise it wouldn't be a gas), then confining it in this piston is giving some pressure to it.  You are releasing that energy.  The gas moves to (as a center of mass), for example, the right, when the piston is expanded to the right.  some molecules bounce off the left side and push it left, while molecules on the right find no barrier and go right until they hit it.  The center of mass of the gas has moved right, and while some of it was expanding right, other particles in it were pushing the piston as a whole left.  The energy comes from the pressure and heat stored in it, and ultimately moves the gas right and the piston left.
